The retrieved evidence shows two incompatible legal and policy positions. In the United States, courts and civil liberties organizations consistently treat hate speech as protected by the First Amendment except in narrow circumstances such as direct incitement to imminent violence or specific threats [d2, d3, d4, d5, d7, d13]. By contrast, several international bodies and national frameworks argue that freedom of speech does not extend to hate speech and support criminalization or regulation to prevent harm and incitement [d1, d9, d10, d12]. Scholarly analyses also differ, with some contending that certain categories of hate speech remain regulable despite being covered by free speech principles [d6, d14].

Because the sources present mutually exclusive claims about whether hate speech falls within freedom of speech protections, the question does not have a single correct answer across jurisdictions and perspectives.
